latin: Nihil magis nociuum theologo quam frequens et assidua in mathematicis Euclidis exercitatio.
translation: Nothing is more harmful to the theologian than frequent and continual practice in the mathematics of Euclid.
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch1, from Latin at farmer1998:23713
doctrine: The conclusion holds that frequent, continual practice in Euclidean mathematics harms the theologian (farmer1998:23713). Cassirer reads it as Pico's conclusion that such practice is harmful to real and genuine knowledge of God (cassirer1942:1099). The neighboring theses set the arts in parallel: music moves the spirits that serve the soul as medicine moves those that govern the body (7>7, farmer1998:23717). Medicine heals the soul through the body, music the body through the soul, in the next conclusion (7>8, farmer1998:23721). Formal, non-material arithmetic, by contrast, gives the best road to natural prophecy (7>9, farmer1998:23724).
context: Mandosio's study of Pico's numerology quotes this conclusion alongside the fourth thesis of the Mathematics section, that the objects of the mathematicians, taken absolutely, perfect the intellect not at all (mandosio2012:411). An unsigned set of notes on Pico's sources for self-knowledge judges Pico 'rather contemptuous of Euclid' even while giving Pythagorean and Platonic mathematics 'a significant place' in his project (selfknowledge_notes:1236). The same notes, citing Pico's ownership of a Greek manuscript of Proclus' commentary on Euclid's Elements, conjecture that his target was the moderni's use of Euclid rather than the ancient commentary tradition (selfknowledge_notes:1237).
historiography: Cassirer quotes the conclusion as evidence that Pico judged mathematical exercise harmful to 'real and genuine knowledge of God' (cassirer1942:1099). Mandosio's article on John Dee's numerology cites the same conclusion within a footnote pairing it with Pico's fourth mathematical thesis (mandosio2012:411). An unsigned set of notes on Pico and self-knowledge is the only source consulted here to comment on the conclusion's target specifically, judging Pico 'rather contemptuous of Euclid' (selfknowledge_notes:1236).
